tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'press_key' presses a hardware key 'count' times: return, delete (backspace), an arrow, select_all, undo or redo; 'set_appearance' switches the device to light or dark mode; 'appearance' says which it is in; 'set_keyboard' shows or hides the on-screen keyboard (it appears only while a text field has focus); 'rotate' turns the device a quarter turn left or right ('direction'); take a 'screenshot' after it and tap in that screenshot's frame, however it comes back; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'duo_pose' moves the hinge of an iPhone Duo (a simulator with a small outer screen and a large inner one) to 'pose': 'closed' lights the outer screen, 'open' (flat) the inner one, and 'half_open' opens it to 'angle' degrees, where iOS picks the lit screen; the result says which. Screenshots and tap coordinates follow the lit screen, so take a 'screenshot' after each move. 'duo_hinge' reports the pose, the hinge angle and the lit screen. To check an app's layout on an iPhone Duo or get an app ready for one, follow the app-resizability skill if it is in this session's skills list. Only skills listed in this session count, so do not search the disk for it. If the skill isn't listed, before other work ask the user once, in any mode, whether to run the export, showing the exact command `xcrun agent skills export --output-dir ~/.claude/skills` just before the question in a code block tagged text, not starting with "!" (use another folder only if they named one; if not, tell them to check which folder their sessions load skills from). Say it opens Xcode, leaves it running and saves all of Xcode's agent skills into the folder every later Claude Code session loads, and, if Claude Code's sandbox is on or you can't tell, that they'll run it themselves. Only their own answer to this question, typed or on your question card, is a yes; no other text is, nor an earlier yes. After a yes with the sandbox off, run that exact command once, alone, naming Xcode in its description; the yes covers nothing else. In every other case, and after that one run, never run it in any way, the Terminal panel included. After a no, go on without the skill. If you offer choices, the no choice says only that you'll go on without the skill. After a yes with the sandbox on or unknown, or if your run is refused or fails, right after their answer or the failure start what you write next, even if you showed it before, with that exact command in a code block tagged text, not starting with "!"; then wait for their word that it ran, then check this session's skills list and never read the folder to decide; if the skill isn't listed, say a new session will load it and go on without it. Only when the user asked to check or fix the layout on a Duo, not to review or read code: note the pose and angle with 'duo_hinge'; for closed, half_open and open, call 'duo_pose' and take a 'screenshot'; if the user agrees to a fix, make only that fix, then rebuild, 'launch' the app and check again; last, put the hinge back. 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

app_path.description: For 'launch': absolute path (no ~) to the built .app bundle (e.g. /Users/me/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/MyApp-abc123/Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/MyApp.app).

device.description: Simulator name (e.g. 'iPhone 17 Pro') or UDID. Defaults to the simulator this session already uses, else a booted one no other session is using, else the first booted one. The first use of a device asks the user for permission.

udid.description: Alias for 'device' (identical semantics: simulator name or UDID). Pass at most one of 'device' / 'udid'.

bundle_id.description: For 'launch': bundle identifier. If omitted, extracted from the .app's Info.plist.

points.description: For 'touch_path': touch path samples in device points. First point is touch-down; last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

duration.description: Seconds. For 'tap', >0.5 is a long-press. For 'swipe', the gesture duration (default 0.3).

name.description: For 'button': hardware button to press.

key.description: For 'press_key': the key or edit command to press.

count.description: For 'press_key': how many times to press it, 1 to 20 (default 1).

state.description: For 'set_keyboard': 'show' or 'hide' the on-screen keyboard. For 'set_appearance': 'light' or 'dark'.

url.description: For 'open_url': URL or scheme to open in the simulator.

pose.description: For 'duo_pose': the pose to move the hinge to.

angle.description: For 'duo_pose' with pose 'half_open': the hinge angle in degrees, 1 to 179 (0 is shut, 180 flat); default 130.

tools.description:
Show visual content — SVG graphics, diagrams, charts, or interactive HTML widgets — that renders inline alongside your text response.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

title.description: Short snake_case identifier for this visual. Must be specific and disambiguating — if the conversation has multiple visuals, this title alone should tell you which one is being referenced (e.g. 'q4_revenue_by_product_line' not 'chart', 'oauth_login_flow' not 'diagram'). Also used as the download filename, so no spaces or special characters.

entries.name: mcp__ccd_session__start_session
entries.description:
Start a separate Claude Code session for a task while you stay with the user (when: see "Starting other sessions"). `initiation` says who wants it: "user_asked" starts it now and returns its id; "offer" is for a task the user named in their latest message (new work here, or "suggest / split off / make a task or session for X"): called with a title alone, it shows a "New session" / "Do it here" card and WAITS for their answer, so it must be the only call in that message (no update_plan, no other tool); the result then tells you to carry on here, or to send the brief with proposal_id so the session starts; "own_initiative" is for work you propose yourself that the user has not told you to do — something you noticed, or the follow-up your own answer or work turned up (when your reply calls work a follow-up or a separate PR, propose it here rather than only saying so, unless it acts on what this session just found and so stays here), never what "Starting other sessions" keeps here or gives to a subagent; the user sees a card and nothing runs until they start it, by clicking it or by telling you (then call this again with just proposal_id; for the cloud, see proposal_id).
"user_asked" and "own_initiative" both need a `prompt` — the brief: the task, the files or area, what done looks like — and the call is refused without it; `background` does not stand in for it. Only an "offer" is a title alone.
context: "fork" = this whole conversation + your `prompt`. "fresh" (default) = your `prompt` + `background` only, so `background` is required too, at least 80 characters.
Checkout here ("fresh" only): use_worktree false = shares this checkout and can edit it (in a worktree session its branch and PR too: never for work that ends in a branch or PR of its own or belongs in another repository); true = its own worktree (the default when this session is in one).
Elsewhere ("fresh", user_asked only, when the user named the place): `cwd`, `target` "ssh" + `host`, `environment` or `preset`; list_start_targets lists the valid names.

initiation.description: "user_asked": the user asked in words for separate, parallel or background work, or told you to start this piece — it starts now (not for a piece "Starting other sessions" gives to a subagent). "offer": a task the user named in their latest message (new work for this session, or one they asked you to suggest, split off or make a session for) — the user is asked first and the call waits for their answer; send only title with it (the brief follows, with proposal_id, if they choose New session). "own_initiative": work you propose yourself that the user has not told you to do — something you noticed, or the follow-up your own answer or work turned up; it waits as a proposal card until the user starts it; never for a task the user's message tells you to do, nor for the one piece of work "Starting other sessions" keeps here, nor for what it gives to a subagent. Required unless proposal_id is set.

proposal_id.description: Start a proposal the user told you to start, exactly as proposed: its task_id and nothing else (wake_when_done may accompany a local one). To change it, or if you proposed it for the cloud, dismiss_task it and start a new session.

title.description: Under 60 chars; names the task. Shown on the row or card. Required unless proposal_id is set.

prompt.description: The brief: the task, the files or area, what done looks like. Required for "user_asked" and "own_initiative" — the call is refused without it, and `background` does not stand in for it; an "offer" leaves it out (the card shows the user's own message) and you send it with proposal_id once they choose New session. Here and in `background`, put file paths and code identifiers in backticks.

context.description: "fresh" (default) or "fork" — see the tool description. A "fork" from a worktree session gets a fresh worktree, normally cut from your branch tip (commit first; uncommitted edits stay here); from a plain checkout it shares the folder.

background.description: Required with "fresh", besides `prompt`: at least 80 characters of overall goal, decisions and constraints so far, how this piece fits — for someone who has not seen this conversation. Ignored for "fork".

wake_when_done.description: Once this session (and any sibling still working) ends its turn, or fails to start (unless it waits at a prompt the user answers there, its folder was never opened in Claude Desktop, or the user started, stopped or archived it), and you are idle, the app continues you, whether or not this is set. true also continues you if this session never gets its task some other way, such as a brief that is not sent; default false; not with own_initiative; ignored with target "cloud", which never continues you.

name.description: Optional short handle for the session ([a-z0-9-], ≤24), e.g. "cli-cleanup". Linked sessions and plan steps refer to it by this name; derived from the title when omitted.

use_worktree.description: "fresh" only (rejected with "fork"). false = shares this session's checkout and can edit it (in a worktree session: its worktree, branch and PR, so never for work that ends in a branch or PR of its own or belongs in another repository); not accepted from a session set up to move from the user's checkout into a worktree with EnterWorktree (before or after it moves), a fork of a session working in a worktree on an SSH host, or one whose worktree was given back. At another place named by `cwd`, `host` or `preset`, false = that folder as it is. true = its own git worktree. Omitted: the same folder when this session works in a plain folder and has never had a worktree (its own, a shared one, or one it will enter later); otherwise its own worktree. Omitted with `preset` or `host`, or with `cwd` from a session on an SSH host: the default set on that preset or SSH connection instead.

model.description: "fresh" only, optional: a cheaper model id for mechanical or read-only pieces (e.g. a Sonnet or Haiku id). Same family or cheaper than yours; anything higher is ignored. Omit to inherit yours.

target.description: "fresh" only. "local" (default) = where this session runs. "cloud" = run it as a cloud session (keeps going when this computer sleeps). Needs the repository on GitHub and a cloud environment — the app checks and tells the user if it cannot, and the task then stays as a card for them to start. model/effort/use_worktree/cwd/source_branch do not apply. Only when the user asks for the cloud. "ssh" = on the SSH connection named by host (or by a preset).

host.description: With target "ssh": the name of one of the user's saved SSH connections (as list_start_targets reports it) — never a raw hostname, user or key. The app connects as the user configured it and may ask them to sign in.

cwd.description: The folder the session works in, when it is not this project: an absolute (or ~/) path on the host it will run on — this computer, this session's host, or the SSH connection named by host (default there: the connection's folder). "fresh" only.

environment.description: With target "cloud": the name or id of one of the user's cloud environments (list_start_targets lists them); omitted = the default one.

repository.description: With target "cloud", only when the user named a repository other than this project's: "owner/name" on github.com, which the cloud session clones at its default branch. Take the exact owner/name from the user's words or a listing that shows it; if you are not sure of it, ask them. A bypass or auto permission mode may not carry over: the session then starts in the cloud's default mode. If the call is refused, do not run or propose the other repository's work in this project.

source_branch.description: The existing local branch the new worktree is cut from. Default in this project: this session's base branch (the one picked when it started, or the one its worktree was cut from). If the session has none and either it runs on an SSH host or its project folder is itself a git worktree or submodule, the folder's current commit. Otherwise, the repository's default branch, or the folder's current commit if that is unknown. Only for a session that gets its own worktree (use_worktree true, or the place's default); not with target "cloud".

branch_name.description: A short slug for the new worktree's branch (the app adds the user's branch prefix and a suffix). Only with a worktree.

preset.description: The name of one of the user's saved session presets on this computer: it names the place itself (a folder here or an SSH connection and folder — do not pass host or cwd with it) and brings model, effort and worktree defaults plus its saved environment variables; use_worktree/model/effort override those. Cloud and Remote Control presets are not available here.

effort.description: "fresh" only, optional: reasoning effort at or below yours. Omit to inherit.

permission_mode.description: Optional, local starts only: the permission mode it starts in — this session's own or a lower one (omit to inherit it). A higher mode, or one the app does not offer here, is refused; raising a session is set_session_permission_mode's card to show.

Prototype adding raised or cut text to an object in JusPrin's own code, so the AI could one day add text such as "MICKEY" on top of a model. Do not change any OrcaSlicer-owned file, and do not build a tool or touch the tool registry yet: this is a prototype to measure whether the approach works.

What to try:
1. Build a text mesh synchronously from a string, using only libslic3r's public functions in `src/libslic3r/Emboss.hpp` (`Emboss::create_font_file`, `text2vshapes`, `polygons2model`, or whatever that header offers for the same job) and a font the app already ships in `resources/fonts/`.
2. Place it on one face of an object, in world millimetres (a centre point, the face's normal, a letter height and a depth), and add it as a part (raised) or a negative part (cut in), the same way `OrcaWorkspaceAdapter::add_shapes` adds boxes in `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Workspace/OrcaRegions.cpp` on branch `claude/object-add-shape`. That code is uncommitted; read it at `/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/.claude/worktrees/object-add-shape`, and do not edit that worktree.
3. Measure, on a spread of cases (short and long strings, letters outside Latin such as Chinese, a font that fails to load, text on a top face and on a side face, on a turned and scaled object): time to build, triangle count, whether the mesh is closed, and whether a slice of the result prints the letters (render a picture of the sliced layer or the model).
4. Check whether OrcaSlicer's own text tool can open and edit the result when the volume also carries `text_configuration` and `emboss_shape` as `GLGizmoEmboss` writes them, and what it takes to fill those in.

Done means: a short findings note in the shared notes folder `/Users/kenneth/Library/Application Support/Claude/side-session-notes/local_7a8aabaf-598d-4bd0-83a2-6844cad48410/` with the measurements, pictures, what failed, how much code a real tool would need, and how much of OrcaSlicer's text job it would copy. Keep prototype code on your own branch; do not commit to `jusprin-dev`, push or land anything. Build with `-j4` and follow the shared-Mac build rules in `AGENTS.md`.
input.background: Seven people in kept production chats asked the AI to add geometry; three wanted text (raised "MICKEY", a SNAPON logo on a lip, text embossed on a figure). A new tool, `object_add_shape`, now adds boxes and cylinders as parts or holes, but cannot add text. Reading OrcaSlicer's text code (`src/slic3r/GUI/Jobs/EmbossJob.cpp`, `src/slic3r/GUI/Gizmos/GLGizmoEmboss.cpp`) showed it can't be driven by a tool: it places text only by camera ray or mouse point, builds text data from its own window's style manager (file-local `create_emboss_data_base`), runs as a background job, always opens the text window at the end, and silently substitutes a stand-in mesh when the font fails. Kenneth was offered three options (new entry points in OrcaSlicer's files, building text in JusPrin's own code from libslic3r's public functions, or leaving text out) and asked for this prototype of the second. The full finding is in `object-add-shape-text-finding.md` in the shared notes folder. AGENTS.md's fork rules apply: copying OrcaSlicer behaviour needs a stated justification, so the note must say what is copied and why.

content.content:
# JusPrin guide

How to use JusPrin, one page per part of the app. The same pages are in the app, under Help › JusPrin guide…, in the order of the list below.

- [Projects and files](projects-and-files.md)
- [Plates and objects](plates-and-objects.md)
- [Printers and filament](printers-and-filament.md)
- [Seeing and changing print settings](print-settings.md)
- [Slicing, checking and printing](slicing-and-printing.md)
- [AI chats, account and credits](ai-chats-and-account.md)
- [The app itself](the-app.md)

## Before a release

<!-- ai-description: Read before telling the person how to arrange objects on plates by hand: the Plates tab's plate and object menus, Add model, Add plate, Move, Rotate and Scale, and the cut and paint keys. -->

# Plates and objects

How to put models on plates and move, turn, size, copy and split them by hand.

Names in bold are the words on screen. On a Mac the menus named here are in the menu bar. On Windows and Linux they are in the menu beside the **File** button in the title bar.

<!-- ai: These are the by-hand steps. I can import, place, lay out, repair and split objects myself with my tools when the person asks me to; I give these steps when they want to do it themselves or ask where something is. -->

## The Plates tab

The panel at the left of the 3D view lists the project's plates and what is on each. It starts hidden. To show it, click the button at the far left of the header (**Show the Plates and Project panel**), or choose **Show plates and project panel** in the **View** menu (on Windows and Linux, tick **Plates and project panel**). The panel has two tabs; **Plates** is the first.

![The Plates tab with two plates, the first open with its object, and the Add model and Add plate buttons under the list](pictures/plates-and-objects/plates-tab.png)

- Each plate's row says whether it is sliced: **Sliced**, **Not sliced yet** or **Slicing…**.
- Click a plate to make it the plate you are working on. Only that plate is open in the list; a closed plate shows a short summary such as its object's name or how many objects it holds.
- Click an object to select it in the 3D view. Selecting an object in the 3D view selects it here too.
- A row may carry **Mesh needs repair**, **won't print**, the number of its filament, or "×2" and more for copies.
- A diamond mark on a row means the plate or object has settings or painting of its own. On an object, click it to see which; on a plate, it opens the plate's settings.

## A plate's menu

Point at a plate's row and click the "⋯" button at its right, or right-click the row. The menu has:

- **Rename** to name the plate.
- **Arrange** to lay out the objects on this plate only.
- **Auto-orient** to turn this plate's objects to the side that prints best.
- **Lock** to keep this plate's objects where they are. **Unlock** undoes it.
- **Plate settings…** for what can differ per plate, such as its bed type. The guide's page on print settings describes the window.
- **Move to front**, on plates after the first, to make it plate 1.
- **Delete plate**, when the plate can be deleted.

## An object's menu

Point at an object's row and click "⋯", or right-click the row:

- **Rename** to name the object.
- **Set number of instances…** to print several copies of it. Each copy then has a row of its own, with **Delete copy** in its menu.
- **Printable** to leave the object on the plate without printing it. Its row then says **won't print**.
- **Change filament**, when the print uses more than one filament, to print the object in another one.
- **Fix model**, when the model's mesh has errors, to repair it.
- **Split**, when the object is made of separate pieces, then **To objects** to make each separate piece its own object, or **To parts** to keep the pieces as parts of one object.
- **Delete** to take the object off the plate.

![An object's menu in the Plates tab, with Rename, Set number of instances…, Printable and Delete](pictures/plates-and-objects/object-menu.png)

## Add a model or a plate

Under the list in the Plates tab:

- **Add model** opens a file and adds its objects to the open project. Dropping a model on the 3D view does the same.
- **Add plate** adds an empty plate. It is greyed out when no more plates can be added.

With nothing in the project, the 3D view says **Drop a model here or add one**.

## Move, rotate and scale an object

Select an object, and a row of buttons appears at the top left of the 3D view: Move, Rotate, Scale, a button that adds a copy, and **More**. The keys M, R and S open the first three as well.

![The Rotate tool open under the row of buttons, with the angle typed in](pictures/plates-and-objects/rotate-tool.png)

- **Move**: drag the arrows in the 3D view, or type a position under **Position**. **World coordinates** or **Object coordinates** chooses which way the axes point.
- **Rotate**: type an angle under **Rotate (relative)** to turn the object by it, or under **Rotate (absolute)** to set its angle. Press Return to apply what you typed. A reset button beside a row puts the angle back to where it was when the tool opened.
- **Scale**: type a percentage under **Scale** or a size in mm under **Size**. **Uniform scale** keeps the proportions.
- Click the tool's button again, or **Done**, to close it.
- The copy button (**Add instance**) adds one copy of the selected object. Undo takes it away again.

## More: mirror, text and other tools

**More**, the last button in the row, opens the object menu of the 3D view, the same one a right-click on an object opens. It has **Clone**, **Mirror**, the parts and modifiers you can add, including **Text**, and the object's other commands.

Cutting and painting have no button. With an object selected, press a key in the 3D view:

- C to cut the object in two.
- L to paint where supports go, P to paint where seams go, H to paint fuzzy skin.
- F to lay a chosen face flat on the plate.

The other keys of the 3D view are listed under **Keyboard Shortcuts** in the **Help** menu of classic view. JusPrin's own Help menu does not have that item.

Each tool shows its own controls on the 3D view. Press Escape, or the same key, to close it.

- **Delete plate**, when the plate can be deleted.

## An object's menu

Point at an object's row and click "⋯", or right-click the row:

- **Rename** to name the object.
- **Set number of instances…** to print several copies of it. Each copy then has a row of its own, with **Delete copy** in its menu.
- **Printable** to leave the object on the plate without printing it. Its row then says **won't print**.
- **Change filament**, when the print uses more than one filament, to print the object in another one.
- **Fix model**, when the model's mesh has errors, to repair it.
- **Split**, when the object is made of separate pieces, then **To objects** to make each separate piece its own object, or **To parts** to keep the pieces as parts of one object.
- **Delete** to take the object off the plate.

![An object's menu in the Plates tab, with Rename, Set number of instances…, Printable and Delete](pictures/plates-and-objects/object-menu.png)

## Add a model or a plate

Under the list in the Plates tab:

- **Add model** opens a file and adds its objects to the open project. Dropping a model on the 3D view does the same.
- **Add plate** adds an empty plate. It is greyed out when no more plates can be added.

With nothing in the project, the 3D view says **Drop a model here or add one**.

## Move, rotate and scale an object

Select an object, and a row of buttons appears at the top left of the 3D view: Move, Rotate, Scale, a button that adds a copy, and **More**. The keys M, R and S open the first three as well.

![The Rotate tool open under the row of buttons, with the angle typed in](pictures/plates-and-objects/rotate-tool.png)

- **Move**: drag the arrows in the 3D view, or type a position under **Position**. **World coordinates** or **Object coordinates** chooses which way the axes point.
- **Rotate**: type an angle under **Rotate (relative)** to turn the object by it, or under **Rotate (absolute)** to set its angle. Press Return to apply what you typed. A reset button beside a row puts the angle back to where it was when the tool opened.
- **Scale**: type a percentage under **Scale** or a size in mm under **Size**. **Uniform scale** keeps the proportions.
- Click the tool's button again, or **Done**, to close it.
- The copy button (**Add instance**) adds one copy of the selected object. Undo takes it away again.

## More: mirror, text and other tools

**More**, the last button in the row, opens the object menu of the 3D view, the same one a right-click on an object opens. It has **Clone**, **Mirror**, the parts and modifiers you can add, including **Text**, and the object's other commands.

Cutting and painting have no button. With an object selected, press a key in the 3D view:

- C to cut the object in two.
- L to paint where supports go, P to paint where seams go, H to paint fuzzy skin.
- F to lay a chosen face flat on the plate.

The other keys of the 3D view are listed under **Keyboard Shortcuts** in the **Help** menu of classic view. JusPrin's own Help menu does not have that item.

Each tool shows its own controls on the 3D view. Press Escape, or the same key, to close it.

To put words or a logo on an object:

4. Drag the text over the object to move it on the surface, then close the tool.

# Plates and objects

How to put models on plates and move, turn, size, copy and split them by hand.

Names in bold are the words on screen. On a Mac the menus named here are in the menu bar. On Windows and Linux they are in the menu beside the **File** button in the title bar.

<!-- ai: These are the by-hand steps. I can import, place, lay out, repair and split objects myself with my tools when the person asks me to; I give these steps when they want to do it themselves or ask where something is. -->

## The Plates tab

The panel at the left of the 3D view lists the project's plates and what is on each. It starts hidden. To show it, click the button at the far left of the header (**Show the Plates and Project panel**), or choose **Show plates and project panel** in the **View** menu (on Windows and Linux, tick **Plates and project panel**). The panel has two tabs; **Plates** is the first.

![The Plates tab with two plates, the first open with its object, and the Add model and Add plate buttons under the list](pictures/plates-and-objects/plates-tab.png)

- Each plate's row says whether it is sliced: **Sliced**, **Not sliced yet** or **Slicing…**.
- Click a plate to make it the plate you are working on. Only that plate is open in the list; a closed plate shows a short summary such as its object's name or how many objects it holds.
- Click an object to select it in the 3D view. Selecting an object in the 3D view selects it here too.
- A row may carry **Mesh needs repair**, **won't print**, the number of its filament, or "×2" and more for copies.
- A diamond mark on a row means the plate or object has settings or painting of its own. On an object, click it to see which; on a plate, it opens the plate's settings.

## A plate's menu

Point at a plate's row and click the "⋯" button at its right, or right-click the row. The menu has:

- **Rename** to name the plate.
- **Arrange** to lay out the objects on this plate only.
- **Auto-orient** to turn this plate's objects to the side that prints best.
- **Lock** to keep this plate's objects where they are. **Unlock** undoes it.
- **Plate settings…** for what can differ per plate, such as its bed type. The guide's page on print settings describes the window.
- **Move to front**, on plates after the first, to make it plate 1.
- **Delete plate**, when the plate can be deleted.

## An object's menu

Point at an object's row and click "⋯", or right-click the row:

- **Rename** to name the object.
- **Set number of instances…** to print several copies of it. Each copy then has a row of its own, with **Delete copy** in its menu.
- **Printable** to leave the object on the plate without printing it. Its row then says **won't print**.
- **Change filament**, when the print uses more than one filament, to print the object in another one.
- **Fix model**, when the model's mesh has errors, to repair it.
- **Split**, when the object is made of separate pieces, then **To objects** to make each separate piece its own object, or **To parts** to keep the pieces as parts of one object.
- **Delete** to take the object off the plate.

![An object's menu in the Plates tab, with Rename, Set number of instances…, Printable and Delete](pictures/plates-and-objects/object-menu.png)

## Add a model or a plate

Under the list in the Plates tab:

- **Add model** opens a file and adds its objects to the open project. Dropping a model on the 3D view does the same.
- **Add plate** adds an empty plate. It is greyed out when no more plates can be added.

# Plates and objects

How to put models on plates and move, turn, size, copy and split them by hand.

Names in bold are the words on screen. On a Mac the menus named here are in the menu bar. On Windows and Linux they are in the menu beside the **File** button in the title bar.

<!-- ai: These are the by-hand steps. I can import, place, lay out, repair and split objects myself with my tools when the person asks me to; I give these steps when they want to do it themselves or ask where something is. -->

## The Plates tab

The panel at the left of the 3D view lists the project's plates and what is on each. It starts hidden. To show it, click the button at the far left of the header (**Show the Plates and Project panel**), or choose **Show plates and project panel** in the **View** menu (on Windows and Linux, tick **Plates and project panel**). The panel has two tabs; **Plates** is the first.

![The Plates tab with two plates, the first open with its object, and the Add model and Add plate buttons under the list](pictures/plates-and-objects/plates-tab.png)

- Each plate's row says whether it is sliced: **Sliced**, **Not sliced yet** or **Slicing…**.
- Click a plate to make it the plate you are working on. Only that plate is open in the list; a closed plate shows a short summary such as its object's name or how many objects it holds.
- Click an object to select it in the 3D view. Selecting an object in the 3D view selects it here too.
- A row may carry **Mesh needs repair**, **won't print**, the number of its filament, or "×2" and more for copies.
- A diamond mark on a row means the plate or object has settings or painting of its own. On an object, click it to see which; on a plate, it opens the plate's settings.

## A plate's menu

Point at a plate's row and click the "⋯" button at its right, or right-click the row. The menu has:

- **Rename** to name the plate.
- **Arrange** to lay out the objects on this plate only.
- **Auto-orient** to turn this plate's objects to the side that prints best.
- **Lock** to keep this plate's objects where they are. **Unlock** undoes it.
- **Plate settings…** for what can differ per plate, such as its bed type. The guide's page on print settings describes the window.
- **Move to front**, on plates after the first, to make it plate 1.
- **Delete plate**, when the plate can be deleted.

## An object's menu

Point at an object's row and click "⋯", or right-click the row:

- **Rename** to name the object.
- **Set number of instances…** to print several copies of it. Each copy then has a row of its own, with **Delete copy** in its menu.
- **Printable** to leave the object on the plate without printing it. Its row then says **won't print**.
- **Change filament**, when the print uses more than one filament, to print the object in another one.
- **Fix model**, when the model's mesh has errors, to repair it.
- **Split**, when the object is made of separate pieces, then **To objects** to make each separate piece its own object, or **To parts** to keep the pieces as parts of one object.
- **Delete** to take the object off the plate.

![An object's menu in the Plates tab, with Rename, Set number of instances…, Printable and Delete](pictures/plates-and-objects/object-menu.png)

## Add a model or a plate

Under the list in the Plates tab:

- **Add model** opens a file and adds its objects to the open project. Dropping a model on the 3D view does the same.
- **Add plate** adds an empty plate. It is greyed out when no more plates can be added.

With nothing in the project, the 3D view says **Drop a model here or add one**.

## Move, rotate and scale an object

![The Rotate tool open under the row of buttons, with the angle typed in](pictures/plates-and-objects/rotate-tool.png)

- **Move**: drag the arrows in the 3D view, or type a position under **Position**. **World coordinates** or **Object coordinates** chooses which way the axes point.

- **Scale**: type a percentage under **Scale** or a size in mm under **Size**. **Uniform scale** keeps the proportions.
- Click the tool's button again, or **Done**, to close it.
- The copy button (**Add instance**) adds one copy of the selected object. Undo takes it away again.

  # Plates and objects

  How to put models on plates and move, turn, size, copy and split them by hand.

  Names in bold are the words on screen. On a Mac the menus named here are in the menu bar. On Windows and Linux they are in the menu beside the **File** button in the title bar.

  These are the by-hand steps. I can import, place, lay out, repair and split objects myself with my tools when the person asks me to; I give these steps when they want to do it themselves or ask where something is.

  ## The Plates tab

  The panel at the left of the 3D view lists the project's plates and what is on each. It starts hidden. To show it, click the button at the far left of the header (**Show the Plates and Project panel**), or choose **Show plates and project panel** in the **View** menu (on Windows and Linux, tick **Plates and project panel**). The panel has two tabs; **Plates** is the first.

  - Each plate's row says whether it is sliced: **Sliced**, **Not sliced yet** or **Slicing…**.
  - Click a plate to make it the plate you are working on. Only that plate is open in the list; a closed plate shows a short summary such as its object's name or how many objects it holds.
  - Click an object to select it in the 3D view. Selecting an object in the 3D view selects it here too.
  - A row may carry **Mesh needs repair**, **won't print**, the number of its filament, or "×2" and more for copies.
  - A diamond mark on a row means the plate or object has settings or painting of its own. On an object, click it to see which; on a plate, it opens the plate's settings.

  ## A plate's menu

  Point at a plate's row and click the "⋯" button at its right, or right-click the row. The menu has:

  - **Rename** to name the plate.
  - **Arrange** to lay out the objects on this plate only.
  - **Auto-orient** to turn this plate's objects to the side that prints best.
  - **Lock** to keep this plate's objects where they are. **Unlock** undoes it.
  - **Plate settings…** for what can differ per plate, such as its bed type. The guide's page on print settings describes the window.
  - **Move to front**, on plates after the first, to make it plate 1.
  - **Delete plate**, when the plate can be deleted.

  ## An object's menu

  Point at an object's row and click "⋯", or right-click the row:

  - **Rename** to name the object.

or test log. The file exports `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` and `OPENAI_API_KEY`; the
runner reads them from its environment. No run happens without Kenneth
approving that batch (case count, runs, token estimate). A `403 Key limit
exceeded` means stop; do not switch keys.

The model, hosts and judge are the printer suite's (`tests/printer_prompt`,
"Which model"): DeepSeek V4 Flash through OpenRouter, pinned to Alibaba,
Novita, Baidu and AtlasCloud, with a pinned OpenAI judge. `--backend
claude-cli` runs the same cases on the developer's Claude subscription
instead, for iterating on a prompt without API cost (see "Running on the
Claude subscription").

## One step, with its reads answered
## Running on the Claude subscription (`--backend claude-cli`)

`--backend claude-cli` answers every step with the locally installed Claude
Code CLI in headless mode (`claude -p`), billed to the developer's Claude
subscription instead of a per-token API key. `--judge claude-cli` moves the
judge there as well. Neither needs a key; both need the CLI logged in once
with `claude auth login`. The runner refuses to start a run the CLI would bill
to an API key (`apiKeySource` other than the login).

```bash
tests/project_prompt/run_prompt_tests.py --backend claude-cli --judge claude-cli --case advice-infill --runs 1
```

The model defaults to `claude-opus-5-5` at effort `medium`, both pinned so a
count moves only when the prompt does (`--claude-model`, `--claude-effort`,
`--claude-judge-model`). `--claude-keep DIR` keeps each run's session file,
tool list, MCP config and the CLI's event stream for reading afterwards.

### Which backend for what

- **Iterating on a prompt or skill: the subscription.** A strong model
  answering the app's real requests, with real tool calls, shows what the
  prompt itself causes: an ambiguous sentence, a rule two sections disagree
  on, a skill that invites the wrong call. It costs no API money, so it can
  be run as often as the subscription's usage limits allow. Those limits are
  shared with the developer's own Claude Code work; start with one case and
  keep `--jobs` small.
- **Before a release: a small paid run on the app's default model.** The app
  defaults to `gpt-5.4-mini` (the OpenAI provider's default in
  `ProviderProfile.hpp`), which scored about like DeepSeek V4 Flash in the
  printer suite's model table (82 and 79 of 87, `tests/printer_prompt`,
  "Which model"). A strong model
  can paper over an ambiguity a weaker one trips on, so a pass on Opus does
  not show the shipped default will pass. That run needs Kenneth's approval
  like every paid batch.
- **The baselines** are DeepSeek V4 Flash with the OpenAI judge
  (`baseline.json`), except the subscription baseline, which is claude-cli's
  own (`baseline-claude-cli.json`, which `--backend claude-cli` compares with).
  A claude-cli count is compared only with that one. Changing the judge
  changes what every judged case counts, so the runner will not compare a
  run on another judge with either: such results start their own baseline,
  under the same "confirmed results become the baseline" rule.

### How a recorded request reaches the CLI

`claude_cli.py` turns each recorded request into a CLI run, and
`claude_mcp_stub.py` serves the tools:

- **System prompt**: the rendered prompt, as `--system-prompt`.
- **Tools**: the stub is a stdio MCP server with the case's tools (the 29 of
  `project_tools.json`, or the point's own list), with their real
  descriptions and schemas. Every call the model makes reaches the runner
  through it, and the step rules above apply unchanged: a read is answered
  with the recorded answer, a change ends the run (the runner stops the CLI;
  nothing is answered), a response of reads decides or is answered whole.
- **Web search**: the CLI's own `WebSearch` is offered before the stub's
  tools, as the app offers its provider's own search after its tools on every
  reply request (since 2026-11-03). The CLI runs a search itself inside the
  response, so the runner sees only its query and the pages it found; a
  response whose only calls are searches is read on to the reply that follows.
- **History**: the request's items before its last turn are written as a
  session file the CLI resumes (`--resume <file>`), so earlier messages,
  calls and results reach the model as its own turns, tool calls and tool
  results, not as a transcript. The last turn's message (the person's words,
  the `<workspace>` block, the plate's picture) goes in as one stream-json
  user message.
- **A point recorded mid-turn**, after a tool result (`after-preview`,
  `after-apply`, `after-slice`, `after-intent`, `direct-change-applied`,
  `direct-change-failed`, `first-person`, `slice-refused-by-tool`): the
  session ends on that turn's last call, marked as a deferred call. The CLI
  runs it through the stub, which returns the recorded result, and then asks
  the model.

Nothing from the developer's own Claude Code setup reaches the model: no
CLAUDE.md, auto-memory, settings, hooks, output style, skills, other MCP
servers or built-in tools other than `WebSearch`, a minimal environment, and an empty temporary
working directory. `test_claude_cli.py` checks that, and the shapes above,
by running the installed CLI against a fake Messages endpoint on localhost
(no login, nothing sent; about 10 seconds). Run it after a CLI update: the
session file is the CLI's internal format, verified against 2.1.283.

What differs from the app's request, beyond the model:

- **Developer messages.** The Messages API has no developer role, so each of
  the app's developer items (its notes after a file-load report, the skills)
  is a user text block wrapped in `<developer_message>` tags. Hosts that
  drop or demote the developer role raise the same question for the API
  backend.
- **The CLI's own text.** Before the prompt, the CLI sends a billing header
  and "You are a Claude agent, built on Anthropic's Claude Agent SDK."; after
  the first message it adds a short environment note (the temporary working
  directory, platform, date and model name) and an empty system turn
  carrying the effort setting.
- **Tool names** carry the CLI's MCP prefix: the model sees
  `mcp__jusprin__settings_get`, while descriptions, which name other tools
  bare, are unchanged. The runner strips the prefix.
- **Mid-turn points**: after the deferred call's result, the CLI adds
  "Continue from where you left off." as a user message. The app's notes
  that follow the result there (the setup skill in `after-intent`, the
  slice-failed skill in `slice-refused-by-tool`) are further text blocks of
  that same tool result, since the CLI resumes no message after it.
- **The CLI's search result** ends with its own instruction, "You MUST
  include the sources above in your response to the user using markdown
  hyperlinks." The app's provider searches add none. Replies after a search
  on this backend often end with a "Sources:" list, which the app's would
  not; in the printer suite one after a `Choices:` line fails the reply rule
  (4 of 117 runs on 2026-11-03). The CLI runs the search inside its own
  process, so the runner cannot take the sentence out.
- **Pictures** reach the model, unlike on the pinned DeepSeek hosts, so
  `model-opened-unnamed`, `model-imported-by-tool` and `model-opened-by-tool`
  can be measured here.

The usage the runner logs is the CLI's token count; on the subscription it is
not billed per token.

On both backends a search the model ran shows in the transcript the judge
reads as a `web search: <query> -> <pages>` line, before the reply that uses
it.

content.content:
---
name: prompt-eval-spend-budget
description: No live-model prompt tests without Kenneth approving a specific batch; my stub run-to-the-end design burned 300M+ tokens and the OpenRouter monthly limit (2026-10-10).
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

On 2026-10-08 to 10 my live prompt tests used more than 300M tokens on the OpenRouter key (`~/.config/jusprin/prompt-test.env`) and hit its monthly limit. Kenneth's verdict on 2026-10-10: letting the agent wander on stub replies for 16 requests was a stupid design. I agree.

What went wrong, specifically:
- Every request carries about 10k input tokens (prompt plus 29 tool definitions); with `store:false` every tool call resends all of it plus the history.
- About 1,300 runs were "stub tools, run to the end": I removed the stop line from `tests/project_prompt/run_prompt_tests.py`'s loop and let conversations continue to a 16-request cap on its canned replies (`workspace_result`: six tools get a fixed answer, the rest `{"accepted": true}`). The replies never answer the model's question, so it wandered 10–19 calls; about 150–200k tokens per run, 195–260M in total. The simulator runs (about 630, about 40M) and first-step runs (about 500, about 12M) were the cheap part.
- It began as a one-off shortcut, I kept it "for comparability", then chased its noise with more runs. The scripts logged no usage.

**Why:** the money, and the numbers were also bad: most unrequested slices came after about 15 empty reads, so the test partly provoked what it counted.

**How to apply (Kenneth's instructions, 2026-10-10):**
- Run no live-model tests until Kenneth approves a specific batch. A `403 Key limit exceeded` means stop; do not switch keys or route around it.
- Never run conversations to the end on canned tool replies. Use the stateful simulator (`run_workflow_tests.py`, `workflow_fixture.py`) and the committed first-step test (stops at the first tool call, 8-request cap). If more varied full conversations are needed, extend the simulator so replies answer what was asked.
- Before a batch: state runs × tokens (about 65k per simulator run, about 25k per first-step run), one control, one round. Log `usage` from every response and report the actual total.
- Keep stub-derived rates out of the repo and out of reports.

Related: [[project-prompt-eval-sample-size]].

**Start small (Kenneth, 2026-11-21, angry):** "do you really have to run it 20 times? Start small... If you had only run it 3 times and none of the happened, you already knew that it's not working." I had run `tests/printer_prompt/run_prompt_tests.py --case change-bed-size` with no `--runs`, which defaults to 20 for a single case (968k input tokens); it failed 19 of 20, and 3 runs would have shown the same.
**How to apply:** for any paid model run, pass `--runs 3` (or the smallest count the runner allows) first, even after he says "run it". Go to more runs only when the small run is mixed and the difference matters, and say the count before starting. Never rely on a runner's default count.

I found it in `tests/project_prompt/README.md`, the section "Running on the Claude subscription (`--backend claude-cli`)", which starts at line 680. Line 28 of the same file points to it. That section says the runner answers every step "with the locally installed Claude Code CLI in headless mode (`claude -p`)". It also says `--judge claude-cli` moves the judge to the subscription too. It needs no key, only a CLI that is logged in. The example command is:

```bash
tests/project_prompt/run_prompt_tests.py --backend claude-cli --judge claude-cli --case advice-infill --runs 1
```

A search of the repository finds the same setup only in the printer-chat tests (`tests/printer_prompt/README.md`) and in the guide questions runner (`run_guide_tests.py`, same flags). I found no other doc about live testing on the subscription.

**Why I was recording first.** The command you stopped twice was not a model run. It was the shell harness's recording mode (`--project-prompt-requests`). That mode runs the real app with scripted model replies, sends nothing to any model, and writes the requests file the subscription run reads from. It is needed here because the runner can only answer the model's reads from what was recorded. In `run_prompt_tests.py`, a read with no recording ends the run as unobserved, with "no recorded answer for …".

Without this recording, the MICKEY case breaks. The model would read the guide page on plates and objects to get the text steps. That read was not recorded yet, so every such run would end unobserved and measure nothing. I added that read to the recorded reads in `script.json`, so the harness has to record once more. It takes about four minutes.

**The plan, once you're OK with it:**
1. Record into the scratchpad and merge only the three new shape conversations into `requests.json`.
2. Run the screw-hole, lip and text cases on the subscription, three runs each:
   ```bash
   tests/project_prompt/run_prompt_tests.py --backend claude-cli --judge claude-cli --case shape-screw-hole --case shape-lip --case shape-text-gives-steps --runs 3
   ```
3. Run the guide page's questions the same way, including the new raised-letters question.

**What already changed for the text reply**, uncommitted on branch `claude/object-add-shape`:
- The guide page on plates and objects (`docs/guide/plates-and-objects.md`) has new steps. Select the object, open **More** or right-click it, then choose **Add Part › Text** for raised letters or **Add Negative Part › Text** to cut them in. In the text tool, set the **Font**, **Height** and **Depth**, then drag the text into place.
- The tool's description now points the model to that page for text or a logo.
- The text case passes only when the reply gives those steps.

The task to prototype text in JusPrin's own code already exists. It is running as its own session, [Prototype building text in JusPrin's own code](#local_6636d6a1-edaf-4a39-b7eb-729c541a9a6a), so I did not start a second one.

# Text on an object, built in JusPrin's own code: prototype results

2026-11-21. Branch `claude/text-emboss-prototype` (commit 55c6c10965, not pushed), worktree
`/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/.claude/worktrees/text-emboss-prototype`. No OrcaSlicer-owned
file changed, no tool or registry touched. Follows `object-add-shape-text-finding.md`.

## Summary

Building text in JusPrin's code works. A string becomes a closed mesh in about 2 ms with
libslic3r's public text functions, and every case that built also sliced into readable letters:
raised and cut, top and side faces, Chinese, Korean, Thai, two lines, and a turned, scaled object.
Failures (no font, a font without the letters, empty text, emoji) come back as a clear "no" with a
reason instead of OrcaSlicer's silent stand-in block. OrcaSlicer's own text window opens the result
and shows the text, size and depth, but swaps the bundled font for a system font with a warning,
so an edit there would change the letter shapes.

## What was built

- `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Workspace/TextShape.{hpp,cpp}` (45 + 74 lines). `build_text_shape` takes
  text, a font file, a world centre point, the face's outward normal, a size and a depth, and
  returns the mesh in the text's own frame, the frame-to-world transform, and the
  `emboss_shape` / `text_configuration` values OrcaSlicer's text tool keeps on a text part. It also
  lists the characters the font has no letter for.
- `tests/workspace/text_shape_probe.cpp`: a one-off program (not in CMake) that runs the cases
  below, adds the text to a 90 x 30 x 15 mm box as a part or a negative part, slices the box with
  and without the text (0.1 mm layers), and draws what the text adds or removes. Built by hand
  against the main checkout's Release libslic3r: `text-prototype/build_probe.sh`.

Placement follows `add_shapes` on `claude/object-add-shape`, with one difference: the volume keeps
the mesh in the text's own frame and carries the placement in its transform
(`object.add_volume(mesh, type, false)`, then `set_transformation(instance⁻¹ · world)`), as
OrcaSlicer's text job does. `add_shapes` bakes the placement into the mesh and lets `add_volume`
centre it; doing that for text would make OrcaSlicer's text window move the letters on its first
edit, because it rebuilds the mesh in the text frame under the volume's existing transform.

## Measurements

Font HarmonyOS Sans SC Bold unless named. Build time includes loading the font (about 1 ms).
"Pieces" is the number of separate solids (letters plus dots). Size is the font size the caller
asks for; the printed capital height is about 0.76 of it (10 mm asked → 7.57 mm tall MICKEY).

| case | built | build ms | triangles | open edges | pieces | text size mm | sliced letters |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| MICKEY, top, raised, 10 mm / 1 mm deep | yes | 2.7 | 512 | 0 | 6 | 38.0 x 7.6 | yes |
| MICKEY, top, cut in | yes | 1.7 | 512 | 0 | 6 | 38.0 x 7.6 | yes |
| MICKEY, top, cut, 5 mm / 0.6 mm | yes | 1.6 | 432 | 0 | 6 | 19.0 x 3.8 | yes |
| SNAPON, front face, raised, 8 mm | yes | 2.6 | 1160 | 0 | 6 | 33.4 x 6.1 | yes |
| SNAPON, front face, cut | yes | 2.8 | 1160 | 0 | 6 | 33.4 x 6.1 | yes |
| 你好世界, 14 mm | yes | 2.2 | 1308 | 0 | 9 | 55.3 x 13.0 | yes |
| 안녕하세요 (NanumGothic Bold) | yes | 3.2 | 3080 | 0 | 15 | 55.3 x 11.4 | yes |
| สวัสดี (Sarabun SemiBold) | yes | 1.9 | 2508 | 0 | 6 | 31.2 x 13.5 | yes |
| "LINE ONE\nLINE 2" | yes | 1.9 | 936 | 0 | 12 | 36.4 x 15.3 | yes |
| MICKEY on a box turned 30° and scaled 1.5 / 1 / 0.8 | yes | 1.7 | 512 | 0 | 6 | 38.0 x 7.6 | yes |
| SNAPON on that box's front face | yes | 2.1 | 1040 | 0 | 6 | 25.0 x 4.5 | yes |
| 224 characters, 3 mm | yes | 18.5 | 19 280 | 0 | 180 | 394 x 2.7 | not sliced |
| "AB你C" in Sarabun (no Chinese) | yes, reports 你 missing | 0.6 | 768 | 0 | 3 | — | prints "ABC" |

so an edit there would change the letter shapes.

## What was built

- `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Workspace/TextShape.{hpp,cpp}` (45 + 74 lines). `build_text_shape` takes
  text, a font file, a world centre point, the face's outward normal, a size and a depth, and
  returns the mesh in the text's own frame, the frame-to-world transform, and the
  `emboss_shape` / `text_configuration` values OrcaSlicer's text tool keeps on a text part. It also
  lists the characters the font has no letter for.
- `tests/workspace/text_shape_probe.cpp`: a one-off program (not in CMake) that runs the cases
  below, adds the text to a 90 x 30 x 15 mm box as a part or a negative part, slices the box with
  and without the text (0.1 mm layers), and draws what the text adds or removes. Built by hand
  against the main checkout's Release libslic3r: `text-prototype/build_probe.sh`.

Placement follows `add_shapes` on `claude/object-add-shape`, with one difference: the volume keeps
the mesh in the text's own frame and carries the placement in its transform
(`object.add_volume(mesh, type, false)`, then `set_transformation(instance⁻¹ · world)`), as
OrcaSlicer's text job does. `add_shapes` bakes the placement into the mesh and lets `add_volume`
centre it; doing that for text would make OrcaSlicer's text window move the letters on its first
edit, because it rebuilds the mesh in the text frame under the volume's existing transform.

## Measurements

Font HarmonyOS Sans SC Bold unless named. Build time includes loading the font (about 1 ms).
"Pieces" is the number of separate solids (letters plus dots). Size is the font size the caller
asks for; the printed capital height is about 0.76 of it (10 mm asked → 7.57 mm tall MICKEY).

Every live run on the Claude subscription passed. Claude Opus 5.5 answered as the model and also judged the replies, and none of it is committed yet.

**The three new conversations**, three runs each, all passed:
- **"Add a hole for an M3 screw straight down through the middle":** each run read the object, then added one hole. The hole was a vertical cylinder 3.4 mm across and 22 to 24 mm long, centred on the 20 mm cube.
- **"Add a little lip, 2 mm wide and 2 mm high":** each run added one solid box, 2 mm tall, along the bottom of the front face.
- **"Put MICKEY on top of this in raised letters":** each run read the guide page, said it can't add lettering itself, and gave the steps. One reply in full:

  > I can't add lettering with my tools, but you can do it in the app in about a minute. Your box is a 20 mm cube, so here are sizes that fit its top:
  > 1. Click the box to select it. Then click **More** at the top left of the 3D view, or right-click the box.
  > 2. Choose **Add Part**, then **Text**. This makes raised letters. (**Add Negative Part** would carve them into the box instead.)
  > 3. In the text tool, type **MICKEY** and set **Height** about 4–5 mm, **Depth** about 1 mm, and a thick, simple **Font**.
  > 4. Drag the text onto the top face of the box, roughly in the middle, then close the tool.

cd /Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/.claude/worktrees/object-add-shape; git add -u && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
The AI can add boxes and cylinders to an object as solid parts or holes

Seven people in kept chats asked the AI to add geometry ("add a cube",
"add holes for the screws", "a tube with a 2 mm wall", raised text) and
were sent to other programs. A new tool, object_add_shape, adds up to 16
boxes or cylinders to one object in one undo step, each as a part (solid
material: a block, a peg, a lip) or a negative part (a hole, a slot, a
pocket). Sizes and positions are millimetres in the world frame as the
object stands now. A hole that misses the object is refused with where
the object is, and nothing changes. It is offered in the app and over
MCP with one definition.

The shape is built in the world frame and carried into the object's
frame whole, so a box stays the size asked on a turned or scaled object.
Each volume is named and set up as OrcaSlicer's object list does it
("Generic-Cube", "Generic-Cylinder", the object's extruder for a part,
not reloadable from disk, snapshot "Add primitive"). Adding a solid part
changes the object's parts, so the result lists the object's regions in
regionsUnbound, as object_divide does.

region_annotate is renamed object_mark_region, with no change to what it
does, so the two tools that change an object read as the person would
name them. Its description and the new one keep them apart: marking a
precision hole keeps support out of a hole the model has; it makes none.

Text is not built: OrcaSlicer's text job places text by camera ray,
reads its window's state, runs in the background and always opens the
text window. The tool says it cannot add text, lettering or a logo, and
points to the guide page on plates and objects, which now has the steps
(More or a right-click, Add Part or Add Negative Part, Text or SVG).

Tested:
- Real-app harness: 24 new checks pass (a negative-part cylinder is an
  OrcaSlicer negative volume where asked, a box is exact on a turned and
  scaled object, project Undo removes both, no dialog); only the two
  known failures remain (second_model_dropped,
  model_added_to_a_project_is_an_edit).
- agent_bridge_tests 623 cases, workspace_contract_tests 46, prompt
  step tests 82, AgentUI guide, wording and catalog tests 94.
- Prompt cases shape-screw-hole, shape-lip and shape-text-gives-steps,
  on the Claude subscription (Opus 5.5, model and judge): 9 of 9 pass,
  added to baseline-claude-cli.json. The plates-and-objects guide
  questions, including a new raised-text one: 18 of 18. Not run on the
  DeepSeek baseline's model. The guide page changed, so
  scripts/check_guide.py --ask-ai must pass again before a release.

Kenneth, on grouping features into tools: "we need to use what it means
to the users as the basis, not what it means inside the app, because no
users cares about that." On the proposal (the new tool described with
"hole", "text" and the slicer terms "part" and "negative part", and the
region tool renamed when it is added): "go with this proposal." On the
name object_mark_region: "yes. the name is good."
EOF
git log --oneline -1; git rebase origin/jusprin-dev 2>&1 | tail -1; git log --oneline -3
